content: Define shot language and camera moves for a neon night market walk-and-talk

**Neon night-market walk-and-talk — shot language & camera moves**

Visual thesis: keep bodies in continuous forward motion while the market *slides past* them. Dialogue rides on the walk; the city is the third character. Neon is not decoration — it is motivated key, bounce, and punctuation.

---

### 1. Grammar (what “shot language” means here)

| Term | Meaning in this scene |
|---|---|
| **Master ribbon** | One long lateral/forward take that holds both speakers and the aisle. Default coverage. |
| **Two-shot in motion** | Both faces readable; market depth behind. Prefer this over ping-pong singles. |
| **Clean single** | One speaker, still walking; use only for a turn, a lie, or a stall. |
| **Over-the-shoulder (OTS) walking** | Foreground shoulder as a moving mask; neon signs smear in bokeh. |
| **Insert / texture** | Hands, steam, hanging ducks, phone glow, puddle reflection — *between* lines, not on them. |
| **Button** | A hold or a lock-off after the last line so the market keeps moving and they don’t. |

**Coverage rule:** story-beat coverage is 100% on the *ribbon* first. Singles and inserts are insurance, not the spine.

**Adjacency:** every shot must match the previous/next on **direction of travel**, **eyeline height**, **screen side**, and **neon color temperature**. Don’t reverse the aisle without a motivated turn or a cut on action (they duck under a lantern, pass a pillar).

---

### 2. Blocking & geography

- **Path:** one continuous aisle, camera-left → camera-right (or vice versa — pick one and keep it). Crowd density high at the edges, a thin “lane” down the middle so the walk never dies.
- **Proximity:** start shoulder-to-shoulder (intimacy / conspiracy). Let a stall or a scooter force a **split** (one character ahead). Rejoin at a beat change.
- **Stops:** 0–1 full stops. Prefer **slow-downs** at a stall (they keep drifting) rather than plant-and-talk. If they must stop, plant on a **practical** (vendor, skewers, ATM glow) so the hold is motivated.
- **Eyelines:** speakers look at each other across a 15–30° angle, not dead profile. In crowds, allow **stolen looks** off-axis (checking a stall, clocking a cop, clocking a rival).

---

### 3. Lenses & camera height

- **Workhorse:** 35mm–40mm equivalent on a full-frame body (or ~25mm Super 35). Wide enough for market depth, tight enough that faces still read.
- **Intimacy / pressure:** 50mm for walking two-shots when the aisle is tight; 85mm for *rare* punch-ins (a secret, a name, a betrayal). Don’t live on the 85 — it kills geography.
- **Texture:** 24mm only for the open (establishing the aisle) and for one “swallowed by the market” beat.
- **Height:** chest-to-eye (not low-hero, not high-surveillance). Dip to waist only for a food/hand insert, then recover.
- **Aperture language:** T2–T2.8. Neon points become discs; faces stay separated from signage. Don’t go so wide-open that continuity of background color is unreadable.

---

### 4. Camera moves (the actual walk-and-talk kit)

**A. Steadicam / gimbal *lateral* (primary)**  
Operator walks parallel in the aisle, slightly ahead or slightly behind, **leading** 70% of the time.  
- Speed: match gait, then *undercrank the operator* half a step so they slightly outpace the characters — creates a gentle push.  
- Axis: keep the lens roughly perpendicular to the direction of travel for a true two-shot; cheat 10–15° toward the speaking face on a line.

**B. Leading walk (front two-shot)**  
Camera backs up the aisle, both faces toward us, market rushing toward the lens. Use for **confession / pitch / “we’re in this.”**  
Watch feet vs. operator; keep a 1.5–2m airbag. If the aisle is too crowded, this becomes the **B-unit** pass, not the master.

**C. Following walk (from behind, ¾)**  
Camera trails ¾ over the listener’s shoulder. Speaker’s face ¾-front in profile-ish. Use when the **listener** is the one changing (doubt, temptation). Neon signs read as streaks over their heads
